extracted.subtask_description: Advice for fiction writers on how to decide which story ideas to pursue, when to abandon or persist, and practical habits to test and develop ideas. Covers mindset, diagnostics, and execution strategies for short stories through novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how the story ends
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t pursue a story unless I know how it ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having an ending prevents quitting by making the work feel finite; the ending retroactively colors the whole book ("the taste left in your mouth"). If you struggle to finish, develop an ending or at least strong end-points before committing to writing. Victoria: she waits months/years until she knows the ending; this helps her never trunk a story once started.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let ideas simmer / keep multiple burners
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat your brain like a multi-burner stove: one project on high heat, others simmering on low while you add ingredients as they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep several projects at varying readiness and add ideas to them over time instead of forcing an immediate choice. Some ideas need long cook times (months to years) to reveal if they have legs. This allows you to pick based on readiness and passion when a slot opens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick projects you’re passionate about
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the idea you are most excited about; passion and excitement drive better writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t choose projects primarily because you think they’ll sell or because you’re chasing market trends. Passion produces better execution; even when under contract you should find a core element in the assignment that excites you so you can commit to writing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to force yourself to write when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcing yourself to write is a separate skill you need when deadlines or contracts demand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you’ve committed to a project, cultivate the ability to be passionate enough about your commitment to produce work on deadline. This is a different discipline than choosing projects by gut-feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution matters more than the seed idea
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea on its own is cheap; the difference is how you execute it across a whole book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard/Dan examples: the same concept can be brilliant or trivial depending on execution (e.g., karaoke/computer-voice vs fully produced song). Stretch and develop the idea—structure, reveals, pacing—to make it work. Be honest about whether you currently have the skill to execute; if not, either develop the skill or adapt the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add ingredients selectively — avoid the kitchen-sink approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t try to put every exciting element into one book; find flavors that work together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withhold tempting bits that would be better showcased in their own story. Learn to identify which elements complement each other and which deserve separate treatments. The 'flavors' metaphor: combine complementary ideas rather than dumping everything into one project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and track ideas (write them down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a record of ideas so they don’t get lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write down ideas (e.g., keep a dream journal next to the bed and review it weekly). If you don’t write ideas down they’re gone; tracking allows you to add ingredients to simmering projects later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice quick fleshing/rapid execution to test ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to execute an idea quickly to see whether it yields something useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard’s TypeCast/illustration example: forcing a fast execution (a minute or two) helps determine whether an idea has potential and trains you to judge ideas quickly. Short experiments can reveal if an idea stretches into a full story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose why you’re struggling before abandoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When you’re stuck, understand whether it’s fear, boredom, health/personal issues, or a real structural problem with the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask diagnostic questions: is this an overarching story problem, a scene problem, a chapter problem, or a 'me' problem (sick, hungry, tired, medication)? Different causes require different fixes. Compile a checklist to run through before deciding to abandon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set mile markers and scenes you’re excited to write
rubrics_metrics.description: Have specific scenes or moments (not just the ending) that you’re excited about to propel you through the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the story has moments spread beyond the first act to look forward to. If bored, refocus by aiming to make the current chapter someone’s favorite—turn chapters into showpieces to keep momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shiny new idea syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of abandoning a current project every time a more alluring new idea appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shiny-new-idea syndrome leads to never finishing anything. Familiarity with material removes initial shine; finishing requires working through that familiarity. Prioritize finishing (especially early-career projects) rather than constantly switching to new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish books to learn and improve
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially early in your career, the goal of a first/early book is to learn how to write your next book; finishing is educational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forcing yourself to finish—even imperfect projects—teaches evaluating and executing ideas more effectively than endless starts. Dan’s anecdote: several unsuccessful novels preceded his first published one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a checklist to evaluate actionable fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a checklist of questions to determine whether the problem is fixable and how to fix it before labeling the work unsalvageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist items include: Is it a story/scene/chapter/me problem? Have I missed a structural element? Do I need rest, hydration, exercise, medication? This reduces premature abandonment by exposing solvable causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon rarely and with reason (compare revision cost vs new writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment should be the exception; one rational reason to shelve is when revising would cost as much as writing a new book and is not likely to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the work would require essentially a rewrite equal to a new novel and success is uncertain, shelving and starting anew may be better. But generally finish and learn from the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify goals for each project
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about what you want the project to accomplish (learn, experiment, sell, build platform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals inform whether to persist or pivot. Early-career goals should emphasize learning/finishing rather than immediate market success. Different goals change the acceptable trade-offs for time/quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest about your skill set and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Know what you can and can’t execute well right now and adapt ideas accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match ideas to current strengths or invest in developing the missing skills. Howard’s example: some ideas are beyond his drawing ability and he either executes differently or doesn’t pursue them. Recognize when execution constraints will sink an idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose which simmering project when slot opens based on present passion
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have an open slot to write, decide among simmering projects by which one currently inspires you most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple projects can be ready at different times; the one you choose often depends on what you feel most excited about in the moment. Contractual deadlines are an exception and may override preference.
